title: HCI Module 2 — Human Information Processing (story explainer)
description: Exam revision told as a story: human factors, task modelling, the human problem-solving model, hierarchical task models, the gulf, memory capacity, context switching and GOMS timing.
endCard: 📘 Human Information Processing — revised. You've got this!

scenes.title: Intro

viz.s: What happens inside your head when you click a button?

lines: Meet Riya. She's typing an assignment, and she wants to change the word Hello into the Times Roman font.
It takes her two seconds. But inside her head, a whole little factory just switched on.
This video is about that factory, how humans process information, and how designers use it to build better interfaces.

scenes.title: 1. Where do interface requirements come from?

items.b: focus interviews and surveys with the target users — the main way to get requirements
general knowledge of how ALL humans work gives a fairly good picture of the user
the human's capability and model of conscious, high-level information processing
how raw signals enter our five senses, are processed to the pre-attentive level, then acted on through the motor organs

lines: Before designing Riya's word processor, designers must understand her. Usually they ask target users directly, with focus interviews and surveys.
But they can also get a fairly good picture from human factors knowledge, facts that are true for almost every human.
Human factors splits into two parts. Cognitive science explains our conscious, high level thinking.
And ergonomics explains the work environment: how raw signals reach our five senses, get processed before we even notice, and turn into action through our muscles.

scenes.title: 2. How human factors helps design

items.b:
write down the steps a human takes to solve a task → the interaction model
observe real users too — cognitive science makes the model much better

predict how people react mentally to different ways of showing information and asking for input → choose the interface
then evaluate models & implementations: explain or predict performance and usability

lines: Human factors helps in two ways. First, task and interaction modelling: writing down the steps a human takes to solve a task.
A careful designer still watches real users, but knowing cognitive science makes the model much better.
Second, prediction, assessment and evaluation. We can predict how people will react to different ways of showing information and asking for input, and choose the interface on that basis.
We can also evaluate an interaction model or a finished interface, and explain or predict its performance and usability.

scenes.title: 3. Interaction = solving a problem

letters.d: goal: a nice-looking document, as easily as possible

lines: Task modelling helps us understand every task needed to reach the system's final goal.
Riya's word processor has a goal: produce a nice looking document as easily as possible. In abstract terms, she's a human solving a problem.
She applies actions on objects. For the small problem of fixing the font, the action is a menu item selection, and the object is the highlighted text.
Keep applying actions to objects, and you arrive at the final solution. So designers can build the interface around this natural problem solving process.

scenes.title: 4. The human problem-solving model (a)
lines: Researchers proposed several human problem solving models, but they all boil down to one picture.
Information from the screen hits Riya's senses. That's sensation. Then perception interprets it: oh, that's the word Hello.
It lands in short term, or working, memory, which constantly swaps knowledge with long term memory.
Then the decision maker decides what to do,
and finally the motor system acts. Her hand clicks the mouse. This chain is the overall information processing model.

scenes.title: 5. Inside the decision maker (b)
lines: Zoom into the decision maker, and it runs a loop. First, define the problem: Hello is in the wrong font.
Gather knowledge: where are the font options?
Consider possible actions: right click? the menu bar?
Create a plan, and execute it.
Observe the results. Did the font change?
If the problem isn't solved, repeat the process. If it is, terminate. Problem solved.
Round and round, until done.

scenes.title: 6. Three important parts

items.b:
sensation senses external info (visual, aural, haptic); perception interprets its basic meaning
lower level — more ergonomic
momentary, short-term and long-term knowledge: the world, procedures, rules, relations, schemas, candidate actions, current objective, the plan
formulates & revises a plan, decides using memory, then acts by commanding the motor system (e.g. left click)

lines: So information processing has three important parts. One: sensation and perception. Sensing visual, aural and haptic input, and pulling out its meaning. This lower level is the ergonomic side.
Two: memory, storing momentary, short term and long term knowledge.
That includes facts about the world, procedures, rules, relations, schemas, candidate actions, the current objective, and the plan.
Three: the decision maker and executor. It forms and revises a plan, decides what to do using memory, and acts by commanding the motor system, like clicking the left mouse button.

scenes.title: 7. A hierarchical task model
lines: Now let's write Riya's task as a tree. At the top: change the font of Hello to Times Roman.
It splits into two subtasks. Select the text: put the cursor left of the letter H, then drag to the right of the letter o.
And change the font: bring up the pop up menu, choose the change font command, then choose Times Roman.
Notice the bottom row. For each of those little subtasks, the designer can choose a specific interface, like a menu, a drag, or a shortcut.

scenes.title: 8. What the tree teaches us

items.b: a task model can be broken down level by level and becomes the basis of the interface structure
choosing an interface for each bottom subtask = the crux (heart) of the HCI design process
the model must reflect what the user expects must be done → the user feels “in tune”
based on ergonomics, user preference, and other requirements or constraints

lines: Lessons from the tree. A task model can be refined level by level, and it becomes the skeleton of the interface.
Choosing an interface for each bottom subtask is the crux, the very heart, of HCI design.
The model must match what the user has in mind, their mental model of what must be done. Then the user feels in tune with the app.
And the interface choice is based on ergonomics, user preference, and other requirements or constraints.

scenes.title: 9. Mental model mismatch — the gulf
lines: Second section: predicting human reaction. Performance has a cognitive side and an ergonomic side. And before acting, a user forms a mental model, much like that hierarchical action plan.
Riya expects the font option to be under right click. But this app hides it under Format, then Text.
That mismatch between the user's mental model and the system's task model creates the gulf. The gulf of execution asks: how do I use this system?
The gulf of evaluation asks: what is the current state of the system? Did anything change?
But when the system's task model maps well to the user's mental model, the gulf closes, and performance becomes very fluid.

scenes.title: 10. Memory capacity

nodes.b: ≈ 8 chunks · very short · rehearsal 🔁 · not transferred → lost

lines: Memory capacity hugely affects performance. Humans have two main types of memory, short term and long term.
Information first passes through sensory memory. If it isn't passed on, it's lost.
Short term memory is also called working memory. It holds changing chunks that matter for the task right now. We hold about eight chunks, for a very short time. Rehearsal keeps them alive.
So an interface can't rely on more than that. Imagine a menu with fifty items. Riya would scan it again and again before choosing.

scenes.title: 11. Story: the online checkout

items.b: present the info again from time to time to refresh memory and prevent errors

lines: Riya is buying shoes online. By the last page, can she remember everything?
The items, the delivery option, which credit card, the billing address, and whether she used a discount card?
That's more than eight chunks. She can't hold it all.
So good checkouts show this information again, from time to time, as a summary. It refreshes her memory and makes sure no errors are made.

scenes.title: 12. Recognition beats recall

items.b:
Type the font name: [ ______ ]
retrieving from long-term memory is difficult and slow

Arial · Calibri · Times-Roman · Verdana
display expert knowledge so users recognise it — even for experts

lines: Getting things out of long term memory is difficult and relatively slow. Typing a font name from memory is hard.
So even if a system targets experts, it should display that knowledge so users can recognise it among options, rather than recall it from scratch.

scenes.title: 13. Multitasking & context switching

nodes.b: working memory full of essay chunks
context switch: working memory replaced; essay state stored back to LTM
capture context on suspension → display, remind, highlight on resumption

lines: Memory also matters in multitasking. Most modern computers let us run many tasks at once.

Riya leaves her essay to answer a WhatsApp message. A context switch happens in her brain. Working memory is replaced with chunks for the new task, and the essay's state goes back to long term memory.
This can degrade overall task performance in many ways.
So a good app helps: it captures the context when you leave, and on your return it displays, reminds and highlights where you were, for fast switching.

scenes.title: 14. Predictive assessment: GOMS

letters.d: what the user wants to accomplish
what the user does to accomplish it
a series of operators that achieve the goal
rules for picking one method when there are several

viz.note: GOMS is a hierarchical task analysis technique — but only measures task performance

lines: Can we predict how fast Riya will be, before she even touches the app? Yes, with GOMS. It's a task analysis technique, in fact a hierarchical task analysis technique.
Goal: what the user wants. Operator: what the user does.
Method: a series of operators that reaches the goal. Selection rules: if there are several methods, how one is chosen.
Remember the limit: GOMS only evaluates task performance, while HCI designs should be judged on many other criteria too.

scenes.title: 15. Table 1 — GOMS time estimates

cells: expert 0.12 s · average 0.20 s · novice 1.2 s
home hands to keyboard or mouse

lines: GOMS comes with time estimates from Card, Moran and Newell. K, keyboard input: point one two seconds for experts, point two for average users, one point two for novices.
T of n, typing n characters: two hundred eighty milliseconds times n.
P, pointing with the mouse: eleven hundred milliseconds.
B, pressing or releasing a button: one hundred milliseconds. B B, a full click: two hundred.
H, moving your hands between keyboard and mouse: four hundred milliseconds.
M, the mental operator, thinking what to do: twelve hundred milliseconds, though it can change.
And W of t: waiting t milliseconds for the system to respond.

scenes.title: 16. How a GOMS evaluation works

nodes.b: same hierarchical task model as before
map an operator (an interface) to each subtask
total time = sum of all subtask times

viz.note: Made for desktops ~30 years ago — still valid, because humans haven't changed

lines: The method: start with the same hierarchical task model.
Map a specific operator, in other words an interface, onto each bottom subtask.
Add up all the times to get the total task time.
Then try different mappings and compare their performance.

GOMS was built for desktops nearly thirty years ago, yet the numbers are still amazingly valid. Computers changed a lot, but human capabilities stayed mostly the same. GOMS models now exist for other environments too.

scenes.title: 17. Story: two ways to delete a file

items.b:
1 point to file icon P
2 click mouse button BB
3 point to file menu P
4 press & hold button B
5 point to DELETE item P
6 release button B
7 point to original window P

1 point to file icon P
2 click mouse button BB
3 move hand to keyboard H
4 hit command-T KK
5 move hand back to mouse H

lines: Let's test it. Riya wants to delete a file. Two designs.
Design one uses menus: point to the file icon, click, point to the file menu, press and hold, point to delete, release, and point back to the window.
Four pointing moves at one point one seconds each, plus the clicks: about four point eight seconds.
Design two is the expert version with a hot key: point to the file, click, move hand to the keyboard, hit command T, and move back to the mouse.
About two point seven seconds. Same task, nearly half the time. That's GOMS helping you choose a design before building it.

scenes.title: Recap

chips: Task tree → pick interface per leaf

lines: Quick recap.
Riya senses, perceives, remembers, decides and acts. Designers model her task as a tree, choose an interface for each leaf, and match her mental model to close the gulf.
Respect her eight chunk memory, let her recognise rather than recall, help her switch tasks, and use GOMS to predict which design is faster. You've got this.
